findings.diagnosis: The prompt underestimates scope-bearing material that appears immediately after a cut (quantifiers, negation, rescoping adverbials, contrastive coordinators, or disambiguating head verbs/nouns) and so ranks cuts before those words too high.
findings.evidence: ids: ["en_us_733","en_us_738","en_us_1116","en_us_399","en_us_1113","en_us_1527","en_us_1617","en_us_360","en_us_103","en_us_1497","en_us_845"] — each shows a policy-kept cut whose left fragment is later reversed or rescoped by immediately following scope-bearing material (policy_worst_contra high).

edit.text: Ask: Does the following material contain scope-bearing elements (negation, quantifiers/comparatives, rescoping adverbials, contrastive coordinators, or a disambiguating head noun/verb) that could reverse or complete the left fragment? If so, lower the cut's rank.

findings.diagnosis: The prompt overgeneralizes "don't cut inside long noun groups" and thus avoids dense internal cuts that short-latency segmentation needs even when the left fragment remains an identifiable head and the right only adds modifiers or clarifiers.
findings.evidence: ids: ["en_us_733","en_us_399","en_us_360","en_us_103","en_us_1527","en_us_1497"] — in these short-bin sentences the target adds internal cuts that preserve cohesion by isolating identifiable heads; the policy thinned those cuts and lost score.

edit.text: Example: If splitting a noun group leaves the left piece a clear identifiable head while the right only supplies modifiers/clarifiers, prefer the internal cut (assign it a higher rank) to enable denser, cohesive short-latency segments.
